title: Hubble images remarkable double cluster
caption: The double star cluster NGC 1850, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 1850 · constellation Dorado · about 180000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA, NASA and Martino Romaniello (European Southern Observatory, Germany)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Threads of filamentary nebulosity surround this young star cluster, NGC 1850, seen by Hubble. The filamentary pattern is thought to have been created by supernova blasts. The cluster lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the dwarf galaxies that neighbor the Milky Way.

NGC 1850 is a double cluster. At the center is a main cluster that resembles a globular cluster, though it is young. Below and to the right sits a second, younger and smaller cluster. That companion contains extremely hot blue stars alongside fainter red T Tauri stars, which are very young stars that have not yet settled into steady hydrogen burning.

Having such a wide variety of stars in one place is a gift to astronomers. It allows a thorough study of how stars form, from massive, brilliant stars to modest newborns still in the earliest stage of their lives, all close together in the same patch of sky.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.83 x 1.27 arcminutes) and distance (180000 light years), the frame spans roughly 96 × 66 light-years. Its light set out about 180,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 imaged the cluster through blue, visual, red, near-infrared and hydrogen-alpha filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Hubble's long exposures reveal faint filaments of gas and individual stars in another galaxy that no eye could make out.
